evidence_quotes.quote: Based on narrative interviews with water users in eThekwini municipality, South Africa the article inquires into how water service delivery matters in terms of people’s lives.

Water Services delivery in eThekwini is characterized by three service levels and several different technological devices. Poor rural areas have been provided with the ground tank system, which guarantees that the free basic water (FBW) is fed daily into a tank in the yard (WSDP, 2004).
Initially a fee was required for the installation of the tank, and some, who could not afford, or did not want to pay, the fee were left out of the programme.
He was not allowed the unlimited option because he was not in possession of a legal contract. The amount of water he could access was written on the cover of the meter, visible to everyone.
The interviewees were encouraged to freely associate with, and speak about, water. They were probed to tell stories about technological artefacts (tanks, meters, standpipes) and tariffs.

What she referred to is that she has to pay for water and that she will face problems of limited access when she is unable to do so. In her case, the death of her husband – the only one with a salary in the family – made it impossible to pay the bills.
The household had its water cut off twice, he told me, but explained that ‘the neighbours help us out. It’s not that bad, we still have water’.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water service delivery and access across rural, township, suburban, flat, and informal settlement communities in eThekwini Municipality (ground tanks, metered connections, flow limiters, and communal standpipes).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines municipal water governance, South Africa's Water Services Act, and Free Basic Water (FBW) implementation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing household water access, including progressive block tariffs and cost-recovery billing rules, FBW volumetric caps, upfront tank installation fees that excluded non-paying households, debt-relief contracts, possession of a legal tenancy/service contract as an eligibility requirement for unrestricted supply versus flow-limiter restriction, and disconnection enforcement.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal and political-ecological empirical study drawing on original fieldwork conducted between November 2008 and April 2009 in eThekwini Municipality, including narrative interviews with 64 domestic water users across six study areas and interviews/correspondence with municipal utility leadership. Per review safeguards, qualitative empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative empirical outcomes directly relevant to household and community water access, including exclusion from ground-tank installation due to upfront fees, multi-day supply interruptions and unreliability, affordability barriers and arrears, volumetric restrictions via flow limiters, exclusion from unlimited water supply for lacking a legal contract, and household service disconnections/cut-offs.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (64 domestic water users and their households/communities across six areas of eThekwini Municipality), exposure (municipal tariff, cost-recovery, FBW, contractual eligibility, fee, and flow-restriction/disconnection rules and devices), outcome (water access, supply continuity, flow restriction, affordability, disconnection, and exclusion), and study design (qualitative narrative interview case study) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study using narrative interviews (fieldwork November 2008 to April 2009)
population_and_sample: 64 domestic water users (individuals/households) interviewed across rural, township, suburban, flat, and informal settlement communities in eThekwini Municipality (Mzinyathi, Inanda, Ntuzuma, Glenwood, Westville, and Crossmoor in Chatsworth), KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, plus municipal water utility management
exposure: Municipal water governance and rule-type access mechanisms under South Africa's Free Basic Water and cost-recovery framework, including progressive block tariffs, upfront tank installation fees, debt-relief agreements, legal contract requirements for unlimited water supply, flow-limiting meters, and disconnection enforcement
outcome: Household and community drinking-water access, exclusion from programme connection due to fees, supply interruptions/reliability, affordability and bill arrears, volumetric flow restriction, and water cut-offs/disconnections (alongside water user subjectivities)
rationale: This full-text qualitative empirical study investigates domestic water access in eThekwini Municipality, South Africa, through 64 narrative interviews conducted in 2008–2009. It satisfies all inclusion criteria: it examines household and community drinking-water service access (c1); analyzes concrete rule-type legal, administrative, tariff, and contractual mechanisms governing access—including Free Basic Water caps, progressive block tariffs, upfront installation fees, debt-relief contracts, legal contract requirements for unrestricted supply versus flow limiters, and disconnections—satisfying both plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings (c2); presents primary qualitative empirical fieldwork (c3); documents concrete access outcomes including exclusion due to fees or lack of legal contract, supply interruptions, affordability struggles, flow restrictions, and disconnections (c4); clearly identifies population, exposure, outcome, and qualitative case-study design (c5); and is written in English (c6). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are explicitly retained for systematic-review mechanism synthesis.
